customer_acme: Hey - we started seeing a bunch of 401s from your API around 2026-03-16 15:12 UTC. Our logs don't show any Redwood request/trace id. What exact bits do you need so you can map this?

emma_support: Sorry about that — we can help map it. Quick checklist of the most helpful items (pick what's easiest for you):
- HAR from the browser (DevTools > Network > Preserve log, then export) OR
- curl reproduction (full request headers + body) OR
- Mobile SDK logs (adb / Xcode device logs) showing the SDK request header
- Approx client timestamp + timezone for the failing request
- If you can generate a debug token in the Console and paste it here, we can look it up from our side.

emma_support: Example minimal curl we can replay (replace placeholders):
```
curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_API_KEY>" \  
  -H "x-redwood-request": "<REQUEST_HASH_FROM_YOUR_SIDE>" \  
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \  
  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \  
  -d '{"input":"hello"}'
```
Note: the header name above is what our SDK emits by default. If your proxy rewrites headers the value may live under a different header name (see below).

emma_support: How to get it fast by client type: 
- Browser: DevTools Network -> find the failing request -> right click -> Save -> Export HAR. Include the request that failed (we need the request headers visible).
- Android (embedded SDK): `adb logcat | grep -i redwood` or `adb logcat -d | grep -E "redwood|rw-req|request-ref"`. SDK logs often print the request hash near the request start.
- iOS (embedded SDK): open Console.app or Xcode device logs, search for `redwood` / `requestId` / `rw-req`. If you can run `idevicesyslog` or upload a sysdiagnose, that helps.

kai_eng: If you sit behind a corporate proxy/load balancer, headers are frequently renamed or stripped. Quick network-side checks: 
- Check your proxy access logs (nginx/apache/ALB) for any header that looks like `x-req-`, `x-request-ref`, `x-redwood-*` or `x-session-hash`.
- If you can capture raw proxy logs, grep for `redwood` or `request` around the client timestamp.
- Example nginx log snippet to capture a forwarded header: `log_format rw '$remote_addr - $remote_user [$time_local] "$request" $status $body_bytes_sent "$http_x_request_ref"';`
If TLS termination is outside your control and you can't see headers, please provide a packet capture from your proxy (or the raw proxy logs) rather than a tcpdump of 443 — the packet capture by itself won't show decrypted headers unless you terminate TLS.

emma_support: For Console debug token (fastest for us to map): Console > Support > Debug tokens > Create token. Set an expiration (we recommend 1 hour), give us the token string and the approximate failure timestamp. Example we expect from you: `DBG-abc123-20260316-1h` (paste the whole token).

customer_acme: Quick update — our edge proxy is rewriting `x-redwood-request` -> `x-req-hash`. I found `x-req-hash: abc123def`. I attached the HAR (network.har). What else do you need?

emma_support: Perfect — thanks. Please also paste the exact client timestamp (with timezone) when you saw the 401 and the curl reproduction (you can redact the API key). If you already created a debug token from the Console, paste that too. We'll map `x-req-hash: abc123def` to our internal span and share the trace. :)

kai_eng: On our side we'll grep logs for the request hash and time window. If we can't find it, we'll ask you for either the HAR request ID (the full request/response pair) or a short pcap from the proxy showing the HTTP request after TLS termination.

customer_acme: Ok attaching HAR + curl (API key redacted) + debug token DBG-xyz789-20260316-1h. Timestamp: 2026-03-16T15:12:38+00:00.

emma_support: Got it, thanks — we'll map and follow up in this thread within 30 minutes. If you want to speed it, reply with your proxy product (nginx/varnish/ALB) and whether TLS is terminated at the proxy or upstream. :thumbsup:
